candidates.source_name: Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle)
candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 48:1 (Exodus (48:1)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee thou didst depart and dwell in the land of Midian five weeks and one year. And thou didst return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee. And thou thyself knowest what He spake unto thee on Mount Sinai, and what prince Mastema desired to do with thee when thou wast returning into Egypt on the way when thou didst meet him at the lodging-place' — Jubilees uniquely identifies the night-encounter at the lodging (Ex 4:24, 'the Lord met him and sought to kill him') as Mastema's attack rather than the Lord's. This is a profound theological clarification: the Mastema-attack reading protects the divine goodness while preserving the canonical narrative. Tewahedo theodicy preserves the Jubilees clarification: episodes ascribed to the Lord in the older canonical text are read as divinely-permitted Mastema-attacks where the moral content of the action would be otherwise inscrutable.

candidates.source_name: Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) / Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle)
candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 48:2 (Exodus (48:2)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And did not he wish with all his power to slay thee, and deliver the Egyptians from thy hand, when he saw thee was being sent to execute judgment and vengeance on the Egyptians?' — Jubilees explicitly names Mastema's motivation: he sought to kill Moses to protect his Egyptian-demonological-fiefdom from the coming judgment. Tewahedo demonological theology preserves this: the demons of false-worship-and-political-oppression are not neutral but actively defend their territorial claim against the deliverer. The canonical pattern (Mastema attempts to kill Moses → Mastema attempts to kill the deliverer at every subsequent moment of canonical-history → Mastema attempts to kill Christ from infancy, cf. Herod) is the Tewahedo demonological-historical reading.

candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 48:9 (Exodus (48:9)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And on the fourteenth day, and on the fifteenth day, and on the sixteenth day, and on the seventeenth, and on the eighteenth day, the prince Mastema was bound and imprisoned behind the children of Israel, that he might not accuse them' — Mastema bound during the Exodus week. Tewahedo Holy-Week theology (Mastema bound during the Paschal mystery; demonic accusation suspended during Christ's Passion-and-Resurrection) draws on Jubilees 48:9 as canonical anchor for the doctrine that the Paschal events constituted demonic suspension of accusation.

'And we permitted them to do all evil deeds, but we did not permit them to be healed by the hands of the Egyptians; and the Lord smote them with malignant ulcers' — Jubilees uniquely preserves the angelic-orchestration of the plagues: the angels of presence permit specific demonic-tormentations against Egypt and explicitly prevent Egyptian healing. Tewahedo angelology reads this as the canonical pattern for the angelic-providential-orchestration of historical-judgment: angels neither cause nor merely-observe judgment but actively manage its scope and persistence. The Tewahedo distinctive Friday-and-Wednesday prayers (the weekly fast-days commemorating Christ's betrayal and crucifixion) include intercessory petitions invoking angelic-orchestration against contemporary historical evils.

'And the Israelites were prepared and ready to be saved, and on the fifteenth day of the third month, even on Passover, they sang a song of praise, having been delivered from the hands of the Egyptians, and from the unclean sea' — Jubilees preserves the Red-Sea crossing-as-Passover-canonical-anchor: deliverance is liturgically datable to Passover. The 'song of praise' detail (Ex 15) is sung in Tewahedo Easter-vigil liturgy preserving the canonical-OT-NT-doubled celebration.

'And in the sixth year of the third week of the forty-ninth jubilee thou didst depart and dwell in the land of Midian five weeks and one year. And thou didst return into Egypt in the second week in the second year in the fiftieth jubilee. And thou thyself knowest what He spake unto thee on Mount Sinai, and what prince Mastema desired to do with thee when thou wast returning into Egypt on the way when thou didst meet him at the lodging-place' — Jubilees uniquely identifies the night-encounter at the lodging (Ex 4:24, 'the Lord met him and sought to kill him') as Mastema's attack rather than the Lord's. This is a profound theological clarification: the Mastema-attack reading protects the divine goodness while preserving the canonical narrative. Tewahedo theodicy preserves the Jubilees clarification: episodes ascribed to the Lord in the older canonical text are read as divinely-permitted Mastema-attacks where the moral content of the action would be otherwise inscrutable.
